title: Erect the Fence
statement:
Each entry `trees[i] = [x_i, y_i]` gives the position of one tree in a garden. A single rope fence of the shortest possible length is stretched so that every tree lies inside it or on it (this fence is the boundary of the convex hull of the trees).

Return the positions of all trees that sit exactly on the fence line, including trees lying on a straight stretch between two corners. When all trees are on one straight line, the fence runs along that line and every tree counts. Each position appears once in the result, and the result may list them in any order.
constraints: All positions in trees are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

The shortest rope around all trees is the convex hull's outline. Testing every pair of trees as a possible fence segment costs O(n³). Andrew's monotone chain does it in O(n log n): sort the points left to right, walk along the bottom and then back along the top, and drop any point where the path turns the wrong way. Trees on a straight stretch of the fence must stay, so only a strict clockwise turn removes a point.

## Approach

1. `cross(o, a, b)` is the cross product of `a - o` and `b - o`: positive for a counter-clockwise (left) turn, negative for a clockwise (right) turn, zero when the three points are collinear.
2. Sort the trees into `points` by `x`, then by `y`.
3. Build `lower` from left to right: before pushing a `point`, pop the last point while the last two points and `point` make a right turn (`cross < 0`).
4. Build `upper` the same way from right to left.
5. Merge both chains, skipping duplicates with `seen` (key `x * 101 + y`), and return `fence`.

## Example 1, step by step

Sorted, `points` is `(1,1) (2,0) (2,2) (2,4) (3,3) (4,2)`. The lower chain pushes `(1,1) (2,0) (2,2) (2,4)`; `(3,3)` makes right turns that pop `(2,4)` and `(2,2)`, and `(4,2)` pops `(3,3)`, leaving `(1,1) (2,0) (4,2)`. Going back, the upper chain ends as `(4,2) (3,3) (2,4) (1,1)`, since `(1,1)` pops `(2,0)` and `(2,2)`. The merge gives `[[1,1],[2,0],[4,2],[3,3],[2,4]]`; only `(2,2)` is inside.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; each point is pushed and popped at most once per chain.
- Space: O(n) for the sorted copy, the two chains and `seen`.

## Pitfalls

- Popping on `cross <= 0` drops trees that sit on a straight edge of the fence; only `cross < 0` may pop.
- When every tree is collinear, both chains contain all of them, so the duplicates must be removed.
- Sorting by `x` alone leaves ties in an arbitrary order and breaks vertical edges; break ties by `y`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cross` | turn direction of `o -> a -> b` (sign of the cross product) |
| `points` | the trees sorted by `x`, then `y` |
| `lower`, `upper` | the bottom chain (left to right) and top chain (right to left) |
| `point` | the tree being added to a chain |
| `seen`, `key` | positions already in the answer, keyed as `x * 101 + y` |
| `fence` | the trees on the fence |

narration.3: Sort a copy of the trees left to right, breaking ties by y, so each chain can be built in one sweep.
narration.5: lower will hold the bottom part of the fence, from left to right.
narration.6: Add the trees one by one in sorted order.
narration.7: If the last two chain points and this tree make a right turn, the middle point dips inside the fence.
narration.8: Drop that middle point; collinear points (cross = 0) are kept because they lie on the fence.
narration.10: The tree joins the bottom chain.
narration.13: upper will hold the top part of the fence, built from right to left.
narration.14: Walk the sorted trees backwards for the top chain.
narration.16: Same rule as before: a right turn means the middle point is inside.
narration.19: The tree joins the top chain.
narration.22: The two chains share their end points (and everything when all trees are collinear), so track what is already in the answer.

narration.26: Only add a tree the first time it is seen.
narration.31: Every tree on the outline, straight stretches included.
